title: How do you implement concurrency control for the "last item / last ticket" problem as a progression — `synchronized`/`ReentrantLock`/`AtomicInteger`/`ConcurrentHashMap` (single JVM only) → DB optimistic/pessimistic locking → Redis distributed lock (`SETNX` + TTL) across many instances → a queue that serializes requests to one consumer (no locks needed)?
shortTitle: How do you implement concurrency control for the "last item / last ticket" problem as a progression

s1_definition.profdef: The "last item" or "last ticket" problem is ensuring that a single remaining unit is sold to exactly one of many concurrent requesters. The solution is a progression of techniques matched to deployment scope: in-process primitives like `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, `AtomicInteger`, or `ConcurrentHashMap` work only within one JVM; database optimistic or pessimistic locking works across many instances sharing one database; a Redis distributed lock with `SETNX` plus a TTL works across instances that do not share a lockable row; and serializing all requests through a queue to a single consumer removes the need for locks entirely.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India is giving away one last festival gift voucher and a hundred customers reach for it at once. If it is a single counter, the teller just uses one hand, no coordination needed, which is like in-JVM locking. If there are many counters sharing one ledger, each teller must check and mark the ledger carefully so two tellers cannot both give it away, which is database locking. If the counters do not share a ledger, they agree on a single talking stick that only one teller can hold, which is the Redis lock. Or the bank simply forms one line that funnels every request to one teller who hands out the voucher in order, which is the queue.
s1_definition.oneliner: For the last unit, use in-JVM locks within one process, database optimistic or pessimistic locking across instances sharing a database, a Redis SETNX lock across instances that do not, or a single-consumer queue that serializes requests so no lock is needed at all.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The "last item" or "last ticket" problem is ensuring that a single remaining unit is sold to exactly one of many concurrent requesters. The solution is a progression of techniques matched to deployment scope: in-process primitives like `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, `AtomicInteger`, or `ConcurrentHashMap` work only within one JVM; database optimistic or pessimistic locking works across many instances sharing one database; a Redis distributed lock with `SETNX` plus a TTL works across instances that do not share a lockable row; and serializing all requests through a queue to a single consumer removes the need for locks entirely.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India is giving away one last festival gift voucher and a hundred customers reach for it at once. If it is a single counter, the teller just uses one hand, no coordination needed, which is like in-JVM locking. If there are many counters sharing one ledger, each teller must check and mark the ledger carefully so two tellers cannot both give it away, which is database locking. If the counters do not share a ledger, they agree on a single talking stick that only one teller can hold, which is the Redis lock. Or the bank simply forms one line that funnels every request to one teller who hands out the voucher in order, which is the queue.

**One line to remember:** For the last unit, use in-JVM locks within one process, database optimistic or pessimistic locking across instances sharing a database, a Redis SETNX lock across instances that do not, or a single-consumer queue that serializes requests so no lock is needed at all.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem is a check-then-act race: every request reads "stock equals one", all decide they can take it, and all decrement, oversELLING to several buyers. Every technique in the progression exists to make the check-and-decrement atomic at a particular scope, and you climb the progression as your deployment grows.

The first rung is in-process concurrency primitives, which only work when exactly one JVM owns the resource. `synchronized` or a `ReentrantLock` serializes the critical section so only one thread checks and decrements at a time. An `AtomicInteger` lets you do a lock-free compare-and-set, for example `if (stock.compareAndSet(1, 0)) grant(); else reject();`, which atomically takes the last unit only if it is still one. A `ConcurrentHashMap` with atomic methods like `compute` or `putIfAbsent` serializes per key. These are the fastest option and are perfect for a single-instance service, but they are useless the moment you run two instances, because each JVM has its own lock and its own AtomicInteger, so both can sell the last unit.

The second rung is database locking, which works across many application instances because they all share one database, and the database becomes the single point of coordination. Optimistic locking uses a version column: you read the stock and its version, then update with `UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?`, and if another transaction already decremented, the version no longer matches, zero rows update, and you retry or reject. It is ideal when conflicts are rare. Pessimistic locking takes a row lock up front with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, so a second transaction blocks until the first commits, then sees the updated stock. It is ideal when contention is high and you prefer waiting over retrying. A simpler and very robust variant is a conditional atomic update, `UPDATE stock SET qty=qty-1 WHERE id=? AND qty>0`, which grants the unit only if stock remains, in one atomic statement.

The third rung is a Redis distributed lock, which you use when instances must coordinate but there is no single lockable database row, for example a one-time external coupon or a resource spread across stores. You acquire a lock with `SET lockKey token NX PX ttl`, where NX means set only if absent so only one caller wins, and PX sets a TTL so a crashed holder's lock expires rather than deadlocking forever. The winner performs the critical operation and releases the lock by deleting it, ideally checking the token so you only delete your own lock. The senior cautions are real: a TTL that is too short can expire mid-operation and let a second holder in, so for strict correctness you use the Redlock algorithm or, better, fence the operation with a monotonic token the resource checks. Because of these hazards you prefer a database constraint over a Redis lock whenever the resource is a row you can constrain.

The fourth rung removes locking entirely by serializing requests through a queue to a single consumer. Every purchase request is published to a queue, and exactly one consumer processes them one at a time in order, decrementing the stock with no contention because there is only ever one actor touching it. This trades some latency and throughput for the simplest possible correctness story and naturally gives you fairness, backpressure, and an audit trail. It is the right choice for extremely high contention flash sales, where even database locks would thrash, because the queue absorbs the spike and the single consumer never races with anyone. The overarching principle is to use the cheapest technique whose scope matches your deployment, and only climb the progression when scaling out breaks the previous rung.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India offers one last discounted fixed-deposit slot and a single-instance service sold it twice under load because two threads both saw one slot. This is exactly the in-JVM rung, where an AtomicInteger compare-and-set takes the last slot only if it is still available.

Problem 2 — When the service scaled to many instances, the in-JVM guard failed because each instance had its own counter. This is exactly the database rung, where a conditional atomic update on the shared stock row enforces single-winner across all instances.

Problem 3 — For a one-time external festival coupon that is not a database row, instances still had to coordinate. This is exactly the Redis-lock rung with SETNX plus TTL.

Problem 4 — During a flash sale the database locks thrashed under extreme contention. This is exactly the queue rung, serializing every request to one consumer.

Our mini-project demonstrates all four rungs. The code defines an `InJvmStock` using AtomicInteger compare-and-set, a `DbStock` using a conditional atomic decrement, a `RedisLock` simulation with SETNX and TTL guarding a coupon, and a `QueueStock` that serializes claims through a single consumer, plus a demo that fires many concurrent buyers at each and shows exactly one winner for the last unit.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one last unit, fifty concurrent buyers released at the same instant, at each rung.

Step 1: At rung one, fifty threads call the in-JVM claim. Each reads the current stock and attempts a compare-and-set from one to zero. Exactly one compare-and-set succeeds because the value can only transition once; the other forty-nine see zero and are rejected. One winner, within this single JVM.

Step 2: At rung two, the same fifty buyers hit the database conditional decrement, simulated by a synchronized row. The first to enter decrements from one to zero and succeeds; every other sees quantity zero and the conditional update affects zero rows, so they are rejected. One winner, and this holds across many instances because they share the one row.

Step 3: At rung three, the coupon has no stock row, so buyers contend on a Redis SETNX lock. One caller sets the key and enters the critical section to redeem, while others fail the NX set and are rejected; the TTL ensures a crashed holder does not deadlock the coupon. One winner across instances.

Step 4: At rung four, all fifty requests are placed on a queue and a single consumer processes them one by one. The consumer grants the first request because stock is one, then rejects the rest because stock is zero, with no lock anywhere because only one actor ever touches the stock. One winner.

Step 5: Every rung reports exactly one winner for the last unit, demonstrating that each technique enforces single-winner at its own scope and that the right rung depends on the deployment.

```
2026-10-24 14:22:10 INFO    RUNG 1 in-JVM winners = 1
2026-10-24 14:22:10 INFO    RUNG 2 DB winners = 1
2026-10-24 14:22:10 INFO    RUNG 3 Redis coupon winners = 1
2026-10-24 14:22:10 INFO    RUNG 4 queue winners = 1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  50 concurrent buyers want the LAST unit
    │
    ├── RUNG 1 (single JVM) ──▶ AtomicInteger.compareAndSet(1→0)
    │        only ONE CAS succeeds ─▶ 1 winner  (breaks if >1 instance)
    │
    ├── RUNG 2 (many instances, shared DB) ──▶ UPDATE qty=qty-1 WHERE qty>0
    │        1 row affected for first, 0 for rest ─▶ 1 winner
    │        (optimistic: WHERE version=? ; pessimistic: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE)
    │
    ├── RUNG 3 (instances, no lockable row) ──▶ SET coupon NX PX ttl
    │        only first SETNX wins ─▶ redeem ─▶ 1 winner  (TTL avoids deadlock)
    │
    └── RUNG 4 (extreme contention) ──▶ enqueue all → single consumer
             consumer decrements in order, NO locks ─▶ 1 winner
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The last-item or last-ticket problem is fundamentally a check-then-act race: many concurrent requests all read that one unit remains, all decide they can take it, and all decrement, so you oversell. Every technique I use exists to make that check-and-decrement atomic at a particular scope, and I describe the solution as a progression where I climb one rung at a time as the deployment grows, always using the cheapest technique whose scope matches the system.

The first rung is in-process primitives, which only work inside a single JVM. A synchronized block or a ReentrantLock serializes the critical section, and an AtomicInteger lets me do a lock-free compare-and-set that takes the last unit only if it is still one, with a ConcurrentHashMap serializing per key. These are the fastest option and perfect for a single instance, but they are useless the instant I run two instances, because each JVM has its own lock and its own counter, so both can sell the last unit. That failure is exactly what pushes me to the second rung.

The second rung is database locking, which works across many instances because they share one database that becomes the single coordinator. Optimistic locking uses a version column and an update guarded by that version, so a losing transaction updates zero rows and retries, which suits rare conflicts. Pessimistic locking takes a row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE so a second transaction blocks until the first commits, which suits high contention. In practice the most robust form is a single conditional atomic update that decrements only where quantity is greater than zero. When instances must coordinate but there is no lockable row, for example a one-time external coupon, I climb to the third rung, a Redis distributed lock using SET with NX and a PX TTL, where NX makes only the first caller win and the TTL prevents a crashed holder from deadlocking the resource forever, and for strict correctness I add a fencing token. The fourth rung removes locking entirely: I push every request onto a queue and let a single consumer process them one at a time, so there is only ever one actor touching the stock and no contention exists, which is the right choice for extreme flash-sale contention because the queue absorbs the spike and also gives fairness, backpressure, and an audit trail.

On my project at National Bank of India I actually walked this progression. A single-instance service sold one last discounted fixed-deposit slot twice, so I started with an AtomicInteger compare-and-set. When we scaled out, that broke because each instance had its own counter, so I moved to a conditional atomic decrement on the shared stock row. For a one-time festival coupon that was not a database row, I used a Redis SETNX lock with a TTL. And during a flash sale when even database locks thrashed, I serialized claims through a Kafka topic to a single consumer. The guiding rule I always state is to prefer a database constraint over a distributed lock whenever the resource is a row I can constrain, because the lock's TTL and expiry hazards are real.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I enforce single-winner for the last unit with in-JVM compare-and-set within one process, database optimistic or pessimistic locking across instances sharing a database, a Redis SETNX-plus-TTL lock across instances with no lockable row, or a single-consumer queue that serializes requests so no lock is needed, and I pick the rung by matching its scope to the deployment and climb only when scaling out breaks the previous one.
